Executive Orders
COLUMBIA, S.C.
— Governor Henry McMaster today announced the appointment of Darline Graham to the United States Senate to fill the vacancy created by the passing of U.S.
Senator Lindsey Graham.
Ms.
Graham will be the first woman to represent South Carolina in the U.S.
Senate.
Darline Graham, a native of Central, S.C., has dedicated her career to public service.
Since 2019, she has served as Commissioner of the South Carolina Commission for the Blind, where she has worked to expand opportunities for South Carolinians who are blind or have low vision to achieve employment and independence.
"Lindsey Graham recognized the greatness of America, the seriousness of his work, and also the value of human and lighthearted spirit.
He understood the hopes, dreams, and needs of his state and delivered for his state every time," said Governor McMaster.
"Today, under the law, it is my duty and honor to name someone to serve in the place of this extraordinary man for the remainder of his term.
It is my honor to ask his little sister, Darline, to finish his work."
Prior to her appointment as Commissioner, Ms.
Graham held roles with Clemson University, the South Carolina Department of Employment and Workforce, a
[...]
habilitation.
She has served the people of South Carolina for nearly 30 years.
In addition to her full-time role as SCCB Commissioner, Ms.
Graham currently serves on the South Carolina State Workforce Development Board and is president-elect of the National Council of State Agencies for the Blind.
Ms.
Graham earned a bachelor's degree from the College of Charleston, a master's degree in rehabilitation counseling, and is a Certified Public Manager.
A wife and mother who lives in Lexington, S.C., Ms.
Graham is the sister of U.S.
Senator Graham.
"Lindsey worked harder than anyone to make our state, country, and world better.
He loved his family and loved serving this state and the country.
He dedicated his life to our country," said Darline Graham.
"It is such a privilege to get to finish some of his important work, and I promise to work hard every day over the next several months to support the president and carry forward the efforts of my brother on behalf of the citizens of South Carolina and the United States."
Under Section 7-19-20 of the South Carolina Code of Laws, the governor is authorized to fill a vacancy in the United States Senate by appointment until a successor is elected.
Ms.
Graham will serve until January 3, 2027, when the new Congress convenes following the November 2026 general election.
Because Senator Graham was the South Carolina Republican Party's nominee for the 2026 U.S.
Senate election, state law allows the Party to hold a special primary election to nominate a candidate to replace Senator Graham on the ballot.
Filing for the special primary election will be open from July 21 through July 28, 2026.
The special primary will be held August 11, with a runoff, if necessary, on August 25.
The general election will proceed as scheduled on November 3, 2026.
Senator Graham represented South Carolina in the United States Senate from 2003-2026.
Before serving in the Senate, he represented South Carolina's Third Congressional District in the U.S.
House of Representatives from 1995-2003.
He was also a member of the South Carolina House of Representatives.

Most appointed senators who run end up winning
Since 1990, more appointed senators who have run to keep their seat have won than lost.
Of the 24 whose elections have been decided, 17 won and seven lost (71% vs.
29%).
Two of those who lost were defeated in a primary; three won their party’s nomination but lost in the general election; and two others advanced as top vote-getters in an all-candidate “blanket” primary but lost the resulting runoff.
Election outcomes haven’t always been so favorable for appointed senators.
Between 1960 and 1989, the Senate had 37 appointees, 29 of whom went on to seek election.
But more of those candidates lost (18, or 62%) than won (11, or 38%).
It’s not uncommon for family members to fill a Senate vacancy
Darline Graham isn’t the first Senate appointee to have a family connection to their predecessor.
Historically, most appointed senators with such ties have been women replacing a husband after he died or resigned from office.
In fact, well into the 1970s, this so-called “widow’s succession,” either by appointment or election, was one of the most common ways for women to enter Congress.
Since 1990, two senators have been appointed to a vacancy created by the death of their husband.
Sen.
Jocelyn Burdick of North Dakota chose not to seek election following the death of Quentin Burdick in 1992 and served just three months.
Sen.

Two other appointed senators since 1990 have succeeded their father.
Both Sen.
Lincoln Chafee of Rhode Island (who replaced the late John Chafee in 1999) and Sen.
Lisa Murkowski of Alaska (who replaced the retiring Frank Murkowski in 2002) subsequently ran for election and won.
Murkowski still holds her seat and was reelected to a fourth full term in 2022.

South Carolina’s U.S.
Senate race was once widely expected to be a Republican win.
It is now a very competitive election.

The latest ECU Poll of South Carolina’s U.S.
Senate race, conducted October 19–24, shows former Republican Senator Darline Graham leading Democratic challenger Annie Andrews by four percentage points among likely voters, 51% to 47%.
Another 2% support an independent, minor-party, or write-in candidate.
The poll has a credibility interval of ±3.7 percentage points, comparable to a margin of error.
Andrews holds a slight advantage in favorability with 44% of respondents reporting a favorable opinion toward her and 36% reporting an unfavorable opinion.
Graham, by comparison, has a 39% favorable rating and a 38% unfavorable rating.
When asked which issue is most important in determining their vote in the upcoming election, the top issue was the economy and/or the overall cost of living at 54%.
Among those who cited this issue as the most important, Andrews leads Graham 56% to 41%.
Additional issues of top concern included border security and/or immigration (14%) and the conflict with Iran and/or other foreign policy issues (7%).
Among those voters who selected border security and/or immigration as the top issue, Graham holds a large advantage over Andrews, 95% to 5%.
Other top issues that respondents selected in the poll included affordability of health care (6%) and crime and/or public safety (6%).
The results of the poll also reveal some notable differences among key segments of the electorate.
Andrews is leading among Independents, 53% to 43%, but Graham leads among male voters by a wide margin of 20 percentage points (59% to 39%).
Andrews does lead the female vote, but by a narrower margin, 54% to 44%.
Additionally, Graham leads among white voters, 67% to 31%.
By contrast, Andrews garners significant support from African American voters, who favor her over Graham by a margin of 88% to 9%.
Graham leads among senior voters (65 years or older) as well, 56% to 43%, whereas Andrews holds a 17-point advantage among younger voters (18 to 29 years old), 58% to 41%.
Voters are further divided by education level.
Among those who are not four-year college graduates, Graham leads by a double-digit margin, 55% to 44%.
Among voters with a four-year college degree, Andrews leads by a narrower margin, 51% to 47%.
In assessing the full results of the poll, Dr.
Peter Francia, Director of the ECU Center for Survey Research, remarked, “South Carolina’s U.S.
Senate race was once widely expected to be a Republican win.
It is now a very competitive election.
Graham’s narrow lead in our poll mainly reflects her strength among Republican voters.
Andrews leads Democrats by a wide margin and is also ahead among independents.
Nonetheless, in this poll, Graham’s Republican margin is enough to put her slightly ahead overall.”
Methodology
This ECU Poll was conducted October 19 through 24, 2026.
The results are based on 955 completed responses to the poll’s questionnaire from South Carolina registered voters who are likely to vote in the 2026 general election.
The survey combined a random sample of registered voters statewide with an online panel used to supplement responses from voters ages 18 to 29, Hispanic voters, and African American voters.
Respondents completed the survey via cell phone using MMS-to-web text (N=413), with the sample provided by ReconMR via L2, and an Interactive Voice Response (IVR) system of landlines only (n=184).
The sampling design intentionally oversampled populations that are traditionally difficult to reach in public-opinion surveys.

Party Divisions of the House of Representatives, 1789 to Present
Political parties have been central to the organization and operations of the U.S.
House of Representatives.
As this chart demonstrates, the efforts of the founding generation to create a national government free of political parties proved unworkable.
Parties demonstrated their worth in the House very quickly in organizing its work and in bridging the separation of powers.
Within a decade House parties absorbed the various state and local factions.
The chart below emphasizes the traditional two-party structure of the United States, with third-party affiliations in the Other column.
Additionally, the numbers of Delegates and Resident Commissioners are reflected in the “Del./Res.” Column for reference.
This chart does not address the party affiliation of these Members as they do not hold voting privileges on the House Floor.
The figures presented are the House party divisions as of the initial election results for a particular Congress.
This means that subsequent changes in House membership due to deaths, resignations, contested or special elections, or changes in a Member’s party affiliation are not included.
The determination of party membership relies upon a number of authoritative sources that include The Biographical Directory of the U.S.
Congress, the House Clerk’s Election Statistics, Congressional Quarterly’s Guide to U.S.
Elections, Michael Dubin’s United States Congressional Elections, and Kenneth Martis’s Historical Atlas of Political Parties in the United States Congress.

After the latest redistricting maneuvers, Kondik calculates, House Republicans are defending eight seats that Trump lost in 2024, and 25 more that he carried with a vote total no more than 4 points higher than his national vote share.
In all, Republicans are defending 10 fewer seats this year (33) than in 2018 (43) where Trump in the previous presidential election either ran behind his national vote total or just slightly above it, according to the Center’s analysis.
Democrats (and most independent analysts) continue to believe the party remains favored to regain the House majority, especially because to do so they need to gain only three seats — far fewer than the opposition party usually wins in midterm elections, especially when the president’s job approval rating is as weak as Trump’s is now.

The battle for control of the House of Representatives in 2026 will be decided primarily in Trump country.
Compared with other recent midterm elections, Republicans this year are defending an unusually small number of House seats that either voted against President Donald Trump in 2024 or backed him only narrowly, according to new calculations shared with CNN by the University of Virginia’s Center for Politics.
That means Democrats have fewer easy pickup opportunities against obviously vulnerable targets than is typical for the party out of the White House during a midterm election.
This Trump-tilted terrain is central to the GOP’s hopes of defying the history of midterm losses for the president’s party and maintaining its slim House majority.
“They are playing on our turf,” said Mike Marinella, spokesperson for the National Republican Congressional Committee.
“We have the fundamental advantage.”
Democrats (and most independent analysts) continue to believe the party remains favored to regain the House majority, especially because to do so they need to gain only three seats — far fewer than the opposition party usually wins in midterm elections, especially when the president’s job approval rating is as weak as Trump’s is now.
But even many Democrats acknowledge that the nature of this year’s battlefield will make it difficult to achieve the sweeping gains many party activists are anticipating — much less approach the 41 seats they netted during the 2018 “blue wave” election during Trump’s first term.
In many ways, the 2026 battle for the House is shaping up as a collision between an irresistible force — the tailwind generated for Democrats by Trump’s high disapproval rating — and an immovable object — the unusually large number of Republicans barricaded into ruby-red House districts.
How presidents are shaping House midterms
One of the most powerful trends of modern US politics is that Americans are treating congressional elections more like parliamentary contests that are less a choice between two individuals than a referendum on which party they want to set the national agend
[...]

Bush displayed relatively less strength in the 2004 presidential race.
This pattern persisted through the blue wave election in 2018.
As in those earlier midterms, the Democratic gains that swept the party back to the House majority were concentrated in districts where Trump two years before had either lost or just slightly exceeded his national performance.
Even by then, there were fewer of those marginal seats than in 2006 or 2010 — but the plausible target list for Democrats was still bigger than it is today.
“The battlefield and the map to the majority in ’18 was substantially larger than it is now,” says Democratic consultant Dan Sena, who ran the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee during the party’s sweep that year.
How Trump shapes the Democrats’ target list
This history frames the challenge facing Democrats in 2026.
Compared with 2018, the number of Republicans in highly vulnerable districts, as measured by the previous presidential vote, has continued to shrink, the Center’s calculations show.
That means to score big gains, Democrats will have to advance further onto hostile terrain than parties usually have done in these recent midterms.
After the latest redistricting maneuvers, Kondik calculates, House Republicans are defending eight seats that Trump lost in 2024, and 25 more that he carried with a vote total no more than 4 points higher than his national vote share.
By comparison in 2018, the GOP had to defend 25 seats that Trump lost and another 18 that he carried with a vote total no more than 4 points above his national percentage.
In all, Republicans are defending 10 fewer seats this year (33) than in 2018 (43) where Trump in the previous presidential election either ran behind his national vote total or just slightly above it, according to the Center’s analysis.
The remaining 187 House Republicans this year, or 85% of their conference, are in districts where Trump ran at least 5 points better than his national 2024 percentage of the vote.
That’s higher than the share of seats the majority party held in such secure terrain before Republicans suffered their big midterm losses in 2006 and 2018, and Democrats were routed in 2010.
“Unless the bottom drops out a bit more for Republicans, it may be difficult for Democrats to realize gains anywhere close to what they had in 2018,” said Geoffrey Skelley, chief elections analyst for Decision Desk HQ, a political website.
“That’s because it matters a lot who holds what districts.”
If anything, heading into the midterm House Democrats hold more politically tenuous seats.
Partially as a result of the redistricting wars, 16 of them now hold seats in districts that Trump carried and another three dozen or so are in districts he lost narrowly to Vice President Kamala Harris.

The race for mayor of Los Angeles is a dead heat as the campaign draws to a close, with a new poll showing incumbent Karen Bass erasing the double-digit lead previously held by Councilmember Nithya Raman.
Raman and Bass now each have 40% of likely L.A.
voters in their camps, with 19% still undecided ahead of the Nov.
3 election, according to the UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies poll, co-sponsored by The Times.
The neck-and-neck contest is a big change from September, when Raman jumped out to an 11-percentage-point lead with support from 39% of likely voters compared with Bass at 28%.
It follows weeks of relentless attacks on Raman by Bass, whom some analysts had predicted would need to campaign more aggressively to close the gap with her challenger.
“It’s certainly a breath of fresh air for Bass to see the race close.
She’ll probably feel the campaign is having the effect she wants it to have, which is to put more focus on Raman and put Raman on the defensive,” said Mark DiCamillo, the director of the Berkeley IGS Poll.
The survey released Wednesday was conducted online in English and Spanish with a sample of 2,197 likely city voters between Oct.
19 and Oct.
25.
It has a margin of error of about three percentage points.
“The momentum in this race is with Karen Bass,” said Alex Stack, a spokesperson for Bass’ campaign.
“Ever since Angelenos got their ballots, Nithya Raman has made headlines for all the wrong reasons — voters know they can’t trust her on public safety and other key issues.”
The Raman campaign cited high unfavorable numbers for Bass in the poll, and noted that the mayor “still can’t get ahead” in voter surveys.
“Bass hasn’t led a poll since August and an aggregate of all publicly available polls continues to show Nithya in the lead,” the Raman campaign said in a news release.
The leveling off of the race, along with the sharp decline in undecided voters, was spurred largely by conservative voters who chose Republican Spencer Pratt in the primary deciding to vote for the mayor in the runoff, said DiCamillo.
In the September Berkeley IGS/L.A.
Times poll, 22% of Pratt voters said they planned to support Bass, while 16% said they favored Raman.
That left a whopping 63% of Pratt voters undecided still.
In the new poll, Bass shot up to 41% of the Pratt vote, while Raman dropped to 14% and 45% were still undecided.
Pratt hasn’t endorsed either candidate in the race and continues to bash both Raman and Bass on social media.
“The Pratt voters are the biggest insertion,” DiCamillo said.
“The question remains, since we’re looking at Pratt voters, 45% remain undecided.
Will they vote?”
Raman trailed Bass in every poll during the primary campaign.
Neither candidate had ever cleared 40% in any of the polls conducted by Berkeley IGS/L.A.
Times.
In the June 2 primary election, Bass received 34% of the vote while Raman received 29%.
Pratt placed third with 26%.
In the new poll, Raman shed support in key areas, including among groups that previously appeared to be leaning toward her.
In the September poll, Raman led among Latinos by 24 percentage points, 45% to Bass’ 21%.
In the October poll, Bass was up to 40% and Raman fell to 43%, leaving the two within the margin of error for that key constituency.
DiCamillo said part of that change had to do with the likely voter population becoming more clear as the election neared, and older Latinos appeared to be a larger portion of the electorate.

Three high school girls all dressed in pink strut up to the outcast in red flannel and tell her what it takes to be popular.
But this isn’t a clip from “Mean Girls” — it’s a campaign video for Los Angeles mayoral candidate Nithya Raman.
The outcast, reminiscent of Lindsay Lohan’s character in the 2004 film, explains how she doesn’t mind being a nonconformist — and then compares herself to Raman and the councilmember’s opposition to raises for Los Angeles Police Department officers.
“I have no problem saying no to systems that don’t serve the people,” the girl in flannel says.
“Like Nithya Raman.”
The micro-drama ad, which has racked up more than 200,000 views on social media, is one way Raman is targeting younger voters in her bid to unseat Mayor Karen Bass in Tuesday’s election.
Another ad, featuring a young couple pleased with improved public transit under a Raman administration, has 400,000 views.
There’s a logic to the campaign’s focus on younger voters.
Raman, 45, is supported by 69% of likely voters between ages 18 and 29, compared with 15% for the 73-year-old Bass, according to the latest Berkeley IGS / Los Angeles Times poll.
Among voters ages 30 to 39, the gap is even wider: 74% for Raman compared with 16% for Bass, the poll found.
Part of Raman’s appeal to younger voters is likely her advocacy for affordable housing and renter protections.
Building more affordable housing is a top priority among younger voters surveyed in the September Berkeley IGS/L.A.
Times poll.
In the June 2 primary, Raman received 37% of the vote to Bass’ 28% in neighborhoods where at least 80% of households rent, according to a Times analysis of election data.
Brandon Whalen-Castellanos, a 32-year-old urban planner, moved to L.A.
from Orange County seven years ago and says he identifies with Raman’s story as someone who moved to L.A.
to “aspire toward their dreams.”
Whalen-Castellanos said he voted for Bass in 2022, viewing her as “a seasoned career and coalition builder.”
“But now,” he said.
“I’m not seeing it.
Establishment politics is not working.”
Bass isn’t ceding the younger cohort to Raman, however.
In an interview at a Panorama City campaign event last week, she pointed to her own beginnings as a young organizer, and said she knows what it’s like to go against the status quo.
“I do understand that there is a sector
[...]
ountability over the LAPD and the agency’s budget, said Bailey Swain, who is president of the group and previously worked for Bass during her 2022 campaign.
In her interview, Raman spoke about how the city’s housing policies disenfranchise Black residents, Swain said, and pledged to change zoning laws to expand affordable housing across the city.
“Nithya not only was very honest and frank about what we’re facing, she was able to quickly name it and say this was racist,” Swain, 25, said.
“It was the ‘yes and’ that really impressed our board.”
The group has about 500 members, Swain said, and the decision to endorse was made by the board.
“People are sick of establishment politics and want to see a change in the status quo,” said Liz Garcia, spokesperson for the Raman campaign.
The campaign partners with content creators, providing access to events and interviews with Raman, Garcia said, as a way to introduce Raman in front of their audiences.
While the Berkeley IGS/L.A.
Times polls show younger voters favoring Raman by a wide margin, supporting a candidate and actually voting for them are two different things.
Young voters historically cast ballots at rates lower than voters over 65.
As of Wednesday, only 13% of eligible voters between ages 18 and 34 have submitted their ballots, compared with 47% of those over 65, according to Political Data Intelligence, a research firm.
Often, the main drivers for higher turnout among younger voters are the competitiveness of the race and the issues dominating the campaign — two things present in the L.A.
mayoral race, said Laura Wray-Lake, a professor of social welfare at UCLA with a focus on younger voter engagement.
“They have to feel like their vote is going to go to a candidate who is going to do something that matters,” she said.
“Young people have a lot of political power, if they choose to use it.”
“You can’t put them in a box,” Wray-Lake added.
“They’re not very predictable in how they’re going to vote, and if they’re going to vote.”
Focusing on issues has been a key to success for City Councilmember Eunisses Hernandez, who won reelection this spring after a competitive primary.
Elected for her first term at age 32, Hernandez, now 36 and the youngest member on City Council, said as she campaigned for a second term she found young people are disillusioned — not apathetic.

The Constitution of the State of Florida as revised in 1968 consisted of certain revised articles as proposed by three joint resolutions which were adopted during the special session of June 24-July 3, 1968, and ratified by the electorate on November 5, 1968, together with one article carried forward from the Constitution of 1885, as amended.
The articles proposed in House Joint Resolution 1-2X constituted the entire revised constitution with the exception of Articles V, VI, and VIII.
Senate Joint Resolution 4-2X proposed Article VI, relating to suffrage and elections.
Senate Joint Resolution 5-2X proposed a new Article VIII, relating to local government.
Article V, relating to the judiciary, was carried forward from the Constitution of 1885, as amended.
Sections composing the 1968 revision have no history notes.
Subsequent changes are indicated by notes appended to the affected sections.
The indexes appearing at the beginning of each article, notes appearing at the end of various sections, and section and subsection headings are added editorially and are not to be considered as part of the constitution.

In the gubernatorial contest, Republican Byron Donalds leads Democrat David Jolly by two percentage points, 49% to 47%, with 4% undecided.
The survey was conducted October 12–19, 2026, via telephone using a random sample of 1,471 likely midterm election voters.
The overall margin of sampling error is +/- 2.81 percentage points.
Jolly holds a 16-point advantage over Donalds among independents, pulling 11% of registered Republicans compared to Donalds’ 5% among Democrats.

Republican candidates hold razor-thin advantages in both the Florida governor and U.S.
Senate races, according to the latest statewide poll released Tuesday by the Public Opinion Research Lab at the University of North Florida.
In the gubernatorial contest, Republican Byron Donalds leads Democrat David Jolly by two percentage points, 49% to 47%, with 4% undecided.
Meanwhile, Republican Sen.
Ashley Moody holds a four-point edge, 49% to 45%, against Democratic challenger Angie Nixon in the U.S.
Senate race, with 5% undecided.
Both leads for Republicans have narrowed since UNF's July poll, which showed Donalds ahead by five points and Moody by eight points.
"Though Donalds enjoys a slight advantage, these numbers suggest a competitive gubernatorial race, similar to the race between Andrew Gillum and Ron DeSantis in 2018, which was won by less than a percentage point.
Given the margin of error, a win by either candidate would be unsurprising," said Dr.
Sean Freeder, a UNF political science professor and faculty director of UNF's Public Opinion Research Lab.
Freeder pointed to President Trump's "near-historic" low approval ratings for the close race in Florida.
READ MORE: 2026 Election: Amendments, referendums and other questions on your midterms ballot — a guide
"Donalds' attempt to win over Black voters does not appear to be working, as Donalds receives just 10% of their support, only slightly more than Senator Moody’s 9%, despite not engaging in nearly as much effort," Freeder added.
Cross-party support and independent voters are playing key roles in keeping the margins tight.
Jolly holds a 16-point advantage over Donalds among independents, pulling 11% of registered Republicans compared to Donalds’ 5% among Democrats.
In the U.S.
Senate contest, Nixon leads independents by 15 points.
“Like Donalds, Moody appears to be in a competitive race, though one that leans more decisively in her favor.
Independents favor Nixon by 15 points, and also appear to be more concerned about Moody’s ties to Hope Florida than Nixon’s ties to socialism,” Freeder noted.
“Given the anti-incumbent mood of swing voters, both Donalds and Moody’s success depends upon Republicans not falling too far behind Democrats in terms of turnout and enthusiasm.”
The Republican Party of Florida filed suit last Friday against the Florida Democratic Party, many of its candidates and a slew of television stations, seeking to stop the airing of a political ad highlighting the leaked grand jury presentment in the Hope Florida scandal.
What topics drive voter preferences?
Florida voters were split depending on the issue.
Jolly leads Donalds on handling data centers (41% to 37%), while Donalds holds the advantage on property insurance (43% to 38%).
The two candidates remain deadlocked on affordability and cost of living, with Jolly at 43% and Donalds at 42%.
Both Republican candidates benefit from higher enthusiasm within their base.
Seventy-seven percent of Donalds’ supporters express strong backing compared to 67% for Jolly.
In the U.S.
Senate race, 79% of Moody’s voters support her strongly compared to 75% for Nixon.
“Both Donalds and Moody enjoy a small but real enthusiasm gap among their voters,” Dr.
Freeder said.
“This is perhaps understandable given that former Republican Jolly may be less appealing to Democratic voters further to the left, and leftist Nixon may alienate moderate Democrats with her positions on the economy and Israel.”
Amendment 3: 14% remain undecided
The survey also polled Amendment 3, a proposed homestead property tax exemption measure.
Fifty percent indicated a "yes" vote—10 points short of the 60% supermajority required for passage—while 30% plan to vote "no" and 14% remain undecided.
The survey was conducted October 12–19, 2026, via telephone using a random sample of 1,471 likely midterm election voters.
The overall margin of sampling error is +/- 2.81 percentage points.

It is the first time in three surveys by the pollster that either candidate has led by more than a tenth of a point.

Ballots cast through Tuesday morning are less than a point apart.
Another 3% picked someone else and 3% are undecided.

Media Release Statement by the Monetary Policy Board: Monetary Policy Decision
At its meeting today, the Board decided to increase the cash rate target by 25 basis points to 4.60 per cent.
Inflation remains elevated and some of the upside risks flagged in August are materialising.
The conflict in the Middle East has broadened and global energy prices are now much higher than had been assumed in the August forecasts.
AI-related demand is driving rapid growth in global prices for technology-related goods.
And there remains pressure on domestic capacity.
Liaison indicates that firms are experiencing cost pressures and are either increasing the prices of their goods and services or looking to do so.
Short-term measures of inflation expectations remain elevated.
And recent inflation outcomes in Australia were stronger than expected at the previous meeting.
Growth in output has slowed but, at the margin, was stronger than expected in the June quarter.
There are signs that growth in consumer spending is easing gradually as expected, although housing prices have fallen in most capital cities and new housing loans have declined noticeably.
Labour market conditions have eased broadly as expected in recent months, and labour market leading indicators are broadly stable.
[...]
d in Australia.
To date, however, growth in Australia’s major trading partners has been stronger than expected, as the boost from AI-related investment has outweighed the adverse effects of the Middle East conflict.
In Australia, weak productivity growth continues to constrain potential growth and there are uncertainties about the economic effects of the downturn in the housing market.
Decision
Since the previous meeting, some of the upside risks to inflation are materialising.
There have been further disruptions to global oil supply and recent data suggest that growth and inflation in Australia have been higher than expected.
Higher fuel prices have partially been passed through to prices of other goods and services.
This inflation impulse is in addition to the effect of capacity pressures in the economy.
The Board remains focused on ensuring that high inflation does not become embedded.
To achieve this, growth in aggregate demand needs to remain subdued for a period to reduce capacity pressures and bring inflation back to target.
The three increases in the cash rate target since the beginning of the year have tightened financial conditions and the economy appears to be slowing.
But inflation is still too high and the Board judged that, in light of recent developments, a further tightening in financial conditions is warranted to support a return of inflation to target in a reasonable period.
The Board will continue to do what it considers necessary to bring inflation sustainably back to target, including increasing the cash rate target further if needed.
Accordingly, the Board will be attentive to the data and the evolving assessment of the outlook and risks to guide its decisions.
Monetary policy is well placed to respond to developments, and the Board is focused on its mandate to deliver price stability and full employment.
Today’s policy decision was unanimous.

The recent inflation outcome had exceeded expectations and liaison revealed widespread cost pressures that firms were either passing into the prices of their goods and services or looking to do so.
Short-term measures of inflation expectations remained elevated.
And GDP growth had, at the margin, been stronger than expected.
The labour market had eased broadly as anticipated but leading indicators were broadly stable.
Members agreed that financial conditions were restrictive but that some indicators could imply that the extent of restriction was only modest.
Bond yields had risen sharply over preceding weeks, owing in part to rising term premia but also at least owing in part to market participants’ assessment that the global neutral real interest rate had risen.
Several central banks had raised their policy rates and markets expected further increases over the period ahead.
Members noted that, while monetary policy in Australia had been tightened earlier than in these other countries, future trends in interest rates in Australia relative to other countries would also have a bearing on the exchange rate, with implications for domestic inflation.
In light of these observations, members considered whether to raise the cash rate target by 25 basis points.
The strongest argument for raising the cash rate target at this meeting was that several of the upside risks identified in August had since materialised or were building.
Members noted that there had been additional signals from the July inflation data that domestic capacity pressures may be more extensive than assumed in the August forecast.
That implication was supported by increasingly prevalent messages from liaison about broad-based cost pressures and growth in unit labour costs remaining higher than judged to be consistent with the inflation target (given continued weakness in productivity growth).
When combined with the slightly stronger-than-expected growth in GDP and signs from leading indicators that labour demand was proving resilient, it was reasonable to conclude that excess demand in the economy was greater than members had previously assessed.
International developments added to the view that upside risks to the inflation forecast had materialised.
The Middle East conflict had escalated and oil prices were substantially above the level 
[...]
from financial markets of a potentially higher global neutral interest rate were correct, it would imply that the current cash rate target of 4.35 per cent was less restrictive that it had been two years earlier.
Moreover, if monetary policy in Australia was unchanged, recent and prospective policy tightening by other central banks could cause financial conditions in Australia to loosen via a depreciation of the exchange rate.
Members briefly considered the arguments in support of leaving the cash rate target unchanged.
These rested primarily on the possibility that downside risks to activity and employment could prove larger than expected.
One reason to assess that was if members judged that falling housing prices could have a larger effect on household spending than assumed.
However, scenario analysis suggested that even relatively large falls in housing prices would have only modest direct effects on activity and spending.
Another was the potential for heightened uncertainty associated with the Middle East conflict to weigh on demand.
And a third was that the effects of the tightening in monetary policy earlier in the year might prove to be larger than factored into earlier forecasts.
Having considered these arguments, all members judged that it was appropriate to increase the cash rate target by 25 basis points at this meeting.
They noted that the August forecasts required a number of favourable developments to occur for inflation to return to target within the projected timeframe and that it no longer appeared likely all of these would eventuate.
Members expressed their concern that excess demand was greater than previously assessed.
And they considered it prudent to reinforce the anchoring of medium-term inflation expectations, given the backdrop of a prolonged period of above-target inflation, the indications from liaison of persistent cost pressures and an economy that, while slowing, continued to display a degree of resilience.
In reaching that conclusion, members acknowledged that the trade-off between inflation and full employment had deteriorated because of global cost pressures.
They confirmed that their strategy was still to return inflation to target in a timely manner, while preserving as many of the gains in employment as possible.
However, executing this strategy in an environment of more persistent adverse supply shocks would require accep
[...]
 slower growth in demand and employment than would otherwise be the case.
Members added that the Board’s task was to stabilise medium-term inflation at the target even if part of the medium-term persistence in inflation is driven by factors beyond the influence of monetary policy.
Finally, members discussed the challenges of judging how large the upside risks to inflation were or could become.
They noted that the outlook for inflation would depend, among other things, on developments in the Middle East, the path of external demand, the extent of domestic capacity pressures and on how that influenced the pass-through of cost shocks and the evolution of inflation expectations.
Members noted that it was possible these factors could continue to place upward pressure on inflation.
Against that backdrop, members agreed that they would remain attentive to incoming data and the evolving assessment of the outlook and risks when making their decisions.
The Board will remain focused on its mandate to deliver price stability and full employment and will continue to do what it considered necessary to achieve that outcome, including increasing the cash rate target further if required.
The decision
The Board decided unanimously to raise the cash rate target by 25 basis points to 4.60 per cent.
Liquidity operations
As a further step in the evolution of the RBA’s liquidity operations framework, members considered a proposal to offer liquidity over longer maturities through regular term repo auctions.
Members noted that the proposal reflected work undertaken over an extended period as part of the ongoing enhancement of the RBA’s operating framework.
The Board endorsed the establishment of Term Repo Operations to complement the RBA’s existing standard liquidity facilities.
Members noted that further information about the purpose and design of Term Repo Operations would shortly be announced.1 It was envisaged that Term Repo Operations would be operational in 2027.
Endnote
1 This information was subsequently released; see https://www.rba.gov.au/mkt-operations/resources/tech-notes/term-repo-operations.html.

polymarket-3499790.text:
4.60 %
Effective date 30 September 2026
Next update 2.30 pm, 3 November 2026

Cash rate target – the key monetary policy decision
We determine monetary policy for the country, which involves setting a target for the cash rate.
What is the cash rate?
The cash rate is the interest rate that banks pay to borrow funds from other banks in the money market overnight.
It influences all other interest rates, including mortgage and deposit rates.
In technical terms, it is the interest rate on unsecured overnight loans between banks (loans banks use to manage their liquidity).
It is our operational target for the implementation of monetary policy.
Learn more about the cash rate target
How do we keep the cash rate close to the target?
Banks can deposit funds with the Reserve Bank overnight and earn a little below the target cash rate.
Banks can also borrow funds from the Reserve Bank at a little above the target cash rate.
The cash rate trades inside this corridor, and the Reserve Bank can also transact in Australia’s money markets to affect the supply and demand for cash to steer the cash rate close to the target.
Learn more about how the Reserve Bank implements monetary policy
Who makes the decision?
The Monetary Policy Board decides whether to change or maintain the cash rate target.
The Board comprises the Governor, Deputy Governor, Secretary to the Australian Treasury and six other members appointed by the Treasurer.
Learn about the role, meetings and members of the Monetary Policy Board
How often does the Monetary Policy Board meet to decide the cash rate?
The Board meets eight times a year to consider monetary policy settings.
These meetings follow the release of key economic data on inflation and economic activity.
View our calendar of important releases
How is the cash rate target announced?
We publish the Monetary Policy Decision media release and cash rate target on our website and to the money market at 2.30 pm (Sydney time) after each Board meeting.
Many news outlets report this important decision in real time.
How does the decision affect you?
The cash rate has a strong influence over interest rates in the economy, such as lending and deposit rates.
In turn, these interest rates influence economic activity, employment and inflation.
This affects all Australians, not just those with a mortgage.
Learn more about the transmission of monetary policy.
What are our monetary policy objectives?
We work to ensure inflation is between 2 and 3 per cent and that there is sustained full employment.
Together, these objectives help to maximise the economic prosperity and welfare of the people of Australia.
What guides the Monetary Policy Board?
The Board uses a framework agreed with the government to guide its monetary policy decisions.
This framework has two objectives: to keep consumer price inflation between 2 and 3 per cent and to achieve sustained full employment.
The Board takes into consideration a wide range of factors, including domestic and international economic and financial conditions, along with the outlook for economic growth and inflation in Australia.
These considerations are published after each Board meeting in a Monetary Policy Decision media release and four times a year in the Statement on Monetary Policy.
View the Bank’s Statement on Monetary Policy
Read the Bank’s Monetary Policy Decisions

Trimmed mean annual inflation was 3.6 per cent in September.
The quarterly movement for the CPI was 1.3 per cent and for the Trimmed mean (pre-October 2025 basis) was 1.0 per cent.

CPI rose 4.3% in the year to September 2026
The Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose 4.3 per cent in the 12 months to September 2026, up from 4.0 per cent in the 12 months to August, according to the latest data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS).
Rachael McCririck, ABS head of price statistics, said: “Housing was the largest contributor to annual inflation in September, rising by 5.2 per cent.”
“Annual inflation of 5.2 per cent for Housing reflected rising costs for both New dwellings and Electricity.
New dwelling prices rose 4.7 per cent in the 12 months to September as builders passed on higher costs for materials and labour.
This is down from 5.4 per cent in the 12 months to August.”
Transport was the second largest contributor to annual inflation in September, rising by 8.7 per cent, due to higher automotive fuel prices.
“On a monthly basis, Automotive fuel prices rose 9.4 per cent in September, compared to a rise of 14.8 per cent in August.
This was driven by higher world oil prices,” Ms McCririck said.
When prices for some items change significantly, measures like the Trimmed mean can give more insights into how underlying inflation is trending without the impact of temporary shocks.
In September, Automotive fuel was excluded from the trimmed mean and this was a key driver of the difference between headline and trimmed mean inflation.
“Trimmed mean annual inflation was 3.6 per cent in September.
Trimmed mean annual inflation in August, as released last month, was 3.6 per cent, but a change in seasonal factors has seen that revised down to 3.5 per cent,” Ms McCririck said.
September quarter 2026 CPI data
This month’s publication includes quarterly indexes and movements for the September quarter 2026.
The quarterly movement for the CPI was 1.3 per cent and for the Trimmed mean (pre-October 2025 basis) was 1.0 per cent.

Testimony Opening Statement to the Senate Economics Legislation Committee (Supplementary Budget Estimates)
Michele Bullock
Governor
Senate Economics Legislation Committee (Supplementary Budget Estimates)
– Videoconference
Good morning, Chair and members of the Committee.
My colleagues and I are here today to answer your questions.
As you know, our purpose is to promote the economic prosperity and welfare of the Australian people, now and into the future.
One way we do this is by setting monetary policy to achieve low and stable inflation and full employment, and by supporting the stability of the financial system.
But we also promote the prosperity and welfare of Australians across the full range of our responsibilities, which include supporting a reliable, efficient and competitive payments system, delivering efficient and effective banking services to Australian government agencies, and providing secure and reliable banknotes to Australians.
Since the Committee’s previous hearing with the RBA in June, the Monetary Policy Board has increased the cash rate target by 25 basis points.
It did this with the goal of returning inflation to target.
This has taken the cumulative increase in the cash rate target this year to 100 basis points.
I will start with some background to these decisions and the outlook for the Australian economy.
I’ll then provide an update on the payments system and cash distribution.
Recent monetary policy decisions and the economic outlook
As you know, the Monetary Policy Board sets monetary policy such that inflation is expected to return to the midpoint of the 2–3 per cent target range.
There is some flexibility around the timeframe over which we meet our inflation objective, to balance this with meeting our full employment objective.
But it is important for the economy that inflation does not diverge from target for too long, since that risks it becoming embedded in inflation expectations, which feeds through to price and wage-setting decisions.
Inflation fell significantly from its peak of 7.9 per cent at the end of 2022 to be within the 2–3 per cent target range for a period in 2024 and 2025.
This followed a significant tightening of monetary policy over 2022 and 2023.
But inflation picked up over the second half of 2025 and has remained above target since then.
Recently, inflation has been around 3½ to 4 per cent in year-ended terms.
The increase in inflation reflects both persistent capacity pressures in the Australian economy and global cost pressures associated with the conflict in the Middle East.
Because of both these factors, inflation is likely to remain elevated for some time.
Our most recent published forecasts – in the August Statement on Monetary Policy – suggested that inflation would not return to around the midpoint of the target range until late 2027.
At the time of the August Board meeting, we assessed that the risks to that outlook were skewed to the upside.
Developments since then suggest that although growth in the Australian economy is slowing as expected, some of the international and domestic upside risks to inflation have materialised or are materialising.
Inflation will therefore likely be higher than was our base case in August.
The conflict in the Middle East has re-escalated and global energy prices are now much higher than had been assumed in the August forecasts.
Oil and related prices have increased sharply again and will add materially to inflation, both directly and indirectly as businesses facing increasing pressures from higher transport and related costs attempt to pass them on.
At the same time, short-term inflation expectations are elevated.
Other global cost pressures have increased.
In addition to the energy price shock, the AI boom and extreme weather events are contributing to upward pressure on a range of agricultural and technology-related prices.
The global AI boom is also driving stronger growth in economies that are key parts of the AI supply chain.
In turn, that is driving higher global prices for some AI-related technologies that are supply constrained.
Importantly though, it is not just these global pressures that are driving inflation in Australia.
While they are certainly compounding the inflation problem, we still see inflation arising from domestic capacity pressures.
Despite the unemployment rate recent
[...]
tly by spending on data centres and renewable energy projects.
The share of the population with a job remains high.
This is a welcome outcome for those individuals, their families and the wider Australian economy.
Conditions in the housing market have softened, reflecting the usual transmission of monetary policy, but also tax policy changes and the broader economic environment.
Housing prices have fallen in most capital cities and new housing loans have declined.
This follows a long period of strong growth, however, underpinned by a structural undersupply of housing.
And housing prices are around 50 per cent higher than they were in early 2020.
Financial stability risks from household borrowing remain contained: while many are facing budget pressures, only a small share of borrowers are in negative equity or facing severe repayment difficulty.
I recognise how challenging it is for those experiencing these issues.
I want to emphasise that, while we expect housing prices to be affected when interest rates rise, monetary policy does not target housing prices.
Rather, what matters is how changes in housing prices affect economic activity, the labour market and, ultimately, inflation.
The Monetary Policy Board will meet next week.
We’ll discuss our assessment of the flow of data and how the risks are unfolding.
A key question is whether the tightening in monetary policy to date will be sufficient to bring inflation back to target in a reasonable time.
We are committed to our mandate to deliver price stability and full employment.
I recognise that higher interest rates can be difficult, particularly for households with mortgages who are also facing cost-of-living pressures.
But we can’t allow high inflation to persist.
High inflation hurts everyone.
It means higher grocery costs, higher rent, and higher electricity bills.
It makes everyone’s pay packets and savings worth less – and it particularly hurts people with lower incomes and little savings.
Monetary policy affects all parts of the economy, not just households with mortgages – it influences the spending, saving and borrowing decisions of all households and businesses.
I am happy to expand on this in the Q&A.
Payments system
Another key responsibility for the RBA is the regulation and oversight of the payments system.
We have completed our review of surcharging and merchant card payment costs.

But in August, we did identify three upside inflation risks, and the first was from a prolonged Middle East crisis.
The second was from the burgeoning AI and tech boom that I know you’ve been talking about a lot at this conference, and everyone is.
And the third was the possibility of even weaker domestic supply constraints.
By September, we judged that those three risks had crystallised.
Oil was back over $100, no end in sight to the war.
AI was going gangbusters, and in the Governor’s words, productivity growth, according to the latest National Accounts in Australia, was doing nothing.
So the Board was unanimous in voting to raise rates, and it said importantly that it stood ready to do more if needed.
Where do we stand today?
Well, we’re a week and a half from the policy meeting, and we’re still finalising our forecast.
So I don’t know for sure, but a few things are clear.
The inflation outlook looks materially worse than we projected in the August report.
I think you could do no worse than start with those three same upside risks.
On the Middle East, oil prices are even higher, about a third higher than we assumed in the August projection.
We have these debates about the so-called crack spread and higher refinery prices, and obviously, there are fewer fiscal interventions now in Australia.
So the Middle East picture looks worse.
AI, well, we’re seeing higher AI prices, tech prices feeding through into CPI, not just here but elsewhere.
We continue to have this extraordinary sequence of positive demand shocks around the world.
And we’re having a boom in data centre construction here in Australia as well.
So that’s upside too.
And then on domestic capacity pressures, well inflation’s been coming in at or a little bit above expectations, despite an apparent easing in the labour market.
Components of CPI that are rising the most are actually the ones most directly linked to capacity pressures like market services.
And we hear from Liaison that cost pressures are the number one consideration for businesses.
We said in the minutes last time, you pointed this out I think in some of your pieces, that the staff were looking at whether we needed to change our judgment on capacity pressures in the labour market again,

And look, that is the central banker’s nightmare.
We can’t allow expectations to shift away from the target.
If that’s a picture on inflation, what’s a picture on activity?
It’s more mixed, clearly.
We need a period of below-trend growth to bring inflation down, and we’re seeing that happening.
We’re seeing some slowing under the pressure of tighter monetary policy, higher oil prices.
The labour data last week, a little bit weaker than people had expected.
We’ve got the housing market obviously undergoing quite a major correction and confidence, particularly in the household sector, is very weak.
But it isn’t all downside.
I talked already about the overseas demand growth, particularly now in Asia, which of course are our major trading partners, being stronger than expected.
And the data centre boom onshore is driving some very big numbers on the business investment side.
So look, monetary policy is working.
Labour market is easing.
Consumption growth is quite tepid.
But there are still pockets of growth and the inflation outlook has deteriorated.
So that’s a pretty tricky balance.
Those are the hard choices I talked about.
The challenge that’s facing the Board, it has done for some time, is do you do more to tackle higher inflation, recognising that that means weaker activity, weaker labour market?
We obviously have a dual mandate.
Or do we hold our horses to protect the labour market, to try and protect some of the labour market, and mindful of the potential that there may be more downside momentum of the economy, but accept the risks in so doing that the upside inflation risk embeds, and that becomes more expensive to deal with?
Those are hard choices.
They’re not where we’d like to be ideally as the central bank, but I think that’s what we’re facing into as we meet the week after next.

prices rise at sharpest rate since August 2022
US business activity growth slowed in October but
remained close to September’s recent high in response to
a further improvement in order books.
Growth rates in both
manufacturing and services remained among the best seen
over the past five years as robust domestic demand was
accompanied by renewed signs of export growth.
Hiring also
remained strong, with employment increasing at the second-
fastest pace for over four years as firms boosted capacity to
meet demand.
However, selling prices rose at the sharpest
rate since August 2022 as companies sought to pass on a
further steep rise in costs to customers.
Output and demand
The headline flash S&P Global US PMI Composite Output
Index slipped from 58.4 in September to 57.6 in October but
remained firmly in strong growth territory.
Despite the fall, the
index still signalled the second-sharpest increase in activity
since March 2022.
Growth dipped lower in both manufacturing
and services, but in both cases the rates of expansion were
a
[...]
ss goods and services was the
largest since August 2022.
The upturn in price pressures was
also broad-based: while services inflation edged up to the
steepest since August 2022, manufacturers’ selling prices
rose at a pace not seen since July 2022, with the rate of
inflation accelerating markedly.
Higher prices reflected a further sharp increase in companies’
costs.
Average input costs measured across both goods
and services rose at the fastest pace since November 2022,
excluding only the rise seen in September.
The surge in cost
pressures was most prominent in manufacturing, though
service sector costs also rose sharply again.
Respondents commonly cited oil-based inputs, energy, fuel
and freight rates as having pushed costs higher, but various
other raw materials including steel, aluminum and copper
were also up in price, often due to tariffs or shortages.
Supplier delivery times lengthened to the greatest extent
since 2022 amid material shortages, low stock levels,
overloaded suppliers, labour shortages, rising back orders and
shipping or import delays.
Service providers also widely noted
higher wage rates and increased utility and insurance costs.
Manufacturing PMI
The S&P Global US Manufacturing PMI rose from 55.9 in
September to 56.0 in October, according to the flash reading,
registering the strongest improvement in operating conditions
since May 2022.
Although production and new orders growth
rates slowed, both remained elevated to register sustained
strong expansions.
Jobs growth meanwhile accelerated
further to reach the highest since March 2012, and input
inventories rose at the fastest rate for four months.
Suppliers’
delivery times meanwhile lengthened to the greatest degree
since July 2022.

Manufacturing activity in the region continued to expand overall, according to the firms responding to the October Manufacturing Business Outlook Survey.
The survey’s indicators for general activity, new orders, and shipments all declined but remained positive this month.
The employment index edged down but continued to suggest overall increases in employment.
The prices paid index moved down, while the prices received index moved higher this month; both continued to indicate overall increases in prices.
The firms continued to expect overall growth over the next six months, but most future indicators declined.
Current Indexes Fall but Remain Positive
The diffusion index for current general activity declined for the second consecutive month, falling from 37.8 in September to 20.9 in October (see Chart 1).
More than 41 percent of the firms reported increases in activity (down from 45 percent last month), and 20 percent reported decreases (up from 8 percent); 27 percent of the firms reported no change in current activity (down from 45 percent).
The new orders index fell 25 points to 4.3 this month.
Almost 39 percent of the firms reported increases in new orders, 34 percent reported decreases, and 22 percent reported no change.
The current shipments index moved down 12 points to 15.3.
The employment index continued to indicate an increase in employment overall but edged down 3 points to 9.1 in October.
Eighteen percent of the firms reported increases, 9 percent reported decreases, and 68 percent reported no change in employment.
The average workweek index declined 11 points to 7.5, its lowest reading since June.
Price Indexes Remain Elevated
The firms continued to report overall increases in prices.
The prices paid index moved down 5 points to 43.2 in October (see Chart 2).
More than 43 percent of the firms reported increases in input prices, 52 percent reported no change, and no firms reported decreases.
The current prices received index rose 9 points to 40.1, its highest reading since May 2025.
More than 41 percent of the firms reported increases in the prices of their own goods (up from 33 percent last month), 52 percent reported no change (down from 66 percent), and 1 percent of the firms reported decreases (unchanged from last month).

The monthly survey of manufacturers in New York State conducted by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.
Business activity rose sharply in New York State in October, according to firms responding to the Empire State Manufacturing Survey.
The headline general business conditions index climbed eighteen points to 25.5, its highest level in nearly five years.
New orders increased markedly and shipments grew.
Unfilled orders rose, delivery times lengthened substantially, and supply availability worsened further.
Inventories increased.
Employment continued to rise modestly and the average workweek rose.
The pace of input and selling price increases remained elevated.
Firms continued to expect conditions to improve in the months ahead, though optimism moderated.
Manufacturing activity expanded strongly in New York State, according to the October survey.
The general business conditions index increased eighteen points to 25.5, its highest reading since December 2021.
The new orders index rose twenty-one points to 23.2, and the shipments index increased sixteen points to 13.1, pointing to a solid increase in orders and shipments.
The unfilled orders index rose eight points to 14.0, and the delivery times index came in at 19.8, suggesting an increase in unfilled orders and significantly longer delivery times.
Inventories increased.

Business Confidence in the United States decreased to 54.50 points in September from 54.60 points in August of 2026.
Business Confidence in the United States averaged 52.82 points from 1948 until 2026, reaching an all time high of 77.50 points in July of 1950 and a record low of 29.40 points in May of 1980.

The ISM Manufacturing PMI edged down to 54.5 in September 2026 from 54.6 in August, compared to forecasts of 55.
Still, the reading continued to point to robust growth in the manufacturing sector, with new orders (55.3 vs 53.7) and employment (52.7 vs 51.2) rising at a faster pace while production slowed slightly (56.7 vs 58.3).
Meanwhile, the Supplier Deliveries Index indicated slowing performance for the 10th month (59 vs 59.3), inventories contracted (48.6 vs 50.6) and backlog of orders rose faster (56.4 vs 51.8).
Price pressures surged (77.9 vs 71.1), driven by increases in steel and aluminum, tariffs applied to many imported goods and increases in petroleum-based products as a result of the Middle East conflict.
"40% of the comments were positive and 60% were negative.
Among negative comments, pricing volatility was mentioned in 46%, tariffs 34%, the Iran war 30% and increasing lead times 21%", according to Susan Spence, Chair of the ISM Manufacturing Business Survey Committee.

THE EMPLOYMENT SITUATION - SEPTEMBER 2026
Both nonfarm payroll employment (+29,000) and the unemployment rate (4.2 percent) changed little in
September, the U.S.
Bureau of Labor Statistics reported today.
Employment in all major industries
changed little over the month.
This news release presents statistics from two monthly surveys.
The household survey measures labor
force status, including unemployment, by demographic characteristics.
The establishment survey
measures nonfarm employment, hours, and earnings by industry.
For more information about the
concepts and statistical methodology used in these two surveys, see the Technical Note.
Household Survey Data
Both the unemployment rate, at 4.2 percent, and the number of unemployed people, at 7.1 million,
changed little in September.
The unemployment rate has remained in a narrow range of 4.1 percent to
4.3 percent since March.
(See table A-1.)
Among the major worker groups, the unemployment rate for people who are Black (7.0 percent)
increased in September.
The jobless rates for adult men (3.9 percent), adult women (3.6 percent),
teenagers (14.5 percent), and people who are White (3.6 percent), Asian (2.9 percent), or Hispanic
(4.7 percent) showed little chang
[...]
 little net change since January.
(See table A-1.)
The number of people employed part time for economic reasons changed little at 4.5 million in
September.
These individuals would have preferred full-time employment but were working part time
because their hours had been reduced or they were unable to find full-time jobs.
(See table A-8.)
In September, the number of people not in the labor force who currently want a job changed little
at 5.8 million.
These individuals were not counted as unemployed because they were not actively
looking for work during the 4 weeks preceding the survey or were unavailable to take a job.
(See
table A-1.)
Among those not in the labor force who wanted a job, the number of people marginally attached to
the labor force decreased by 236,000 to 1.5 million in September.
These individuals wanted and were
available for work and had looked for a job sometime in the prior 12 months but had not looked for
work in the 4 weeks preceding the survey.
The number of discouraged workers, a subset of the
marginally attached who believed that no jobs were available for them, changed little over the
month at 414,000.
(See Summary table A.)
Establishment Survey Data
Total nonfarm payroll employment changed little in September (+29,000), following an average
monthly gain of 45,000 over the prior 12 months.
Employment in all major industries changed little
over the month.
(See table B-1.)
Health care employment continued its upward trend in September (+17,000), but at a slower pace than
the average monthly gain over the prior 12 months (+33,000).
In September, employment continued to
trend up in ambulatory health care services (+13,000) and in hospitals (+12,000), while nursing and
residential care facilities lost jobs (-9,000).
Employment in construction changed little in September (+11,000).
The industry had added an average
of 10,000 jobs per month over the prior 12 months.
In September, employment in nonresidential
specialty trade contractors continued to trend up (+12,000).
Manufacturing employment was little changed in September (+9,000) but is up by 72,000 since a
recent low in December 2025.
Over the month, employment increased in plastics and rubber products
manufacturing (+5,000) and in machinery manufacturing (+5,000).
In September, financial activities employment was little changed (-7,000).
Employment in financial
activities is down by 129,000 since a recent peak in May 2025, with most of the job loss in
insurance carriers and related activities (-90,000).
Employment also showed little change over the month in other major industries, including mining,
quarrying, and oil and gas extraction; wholesale trade; retail trade; transportation and
warehousing; information; professional and business services; social assistance; leisure and
hospitality; other services; and government.
In September, average hourly earnings for all employees on private nonfarm payrolls edged up by 5
cents, or 0.1 percent, to $37.81.
Over the past 12 months, average hourly earnings have increased
by 3.0 percent.
In September, average hourly earnings of private-sector production and
nonsupervisory employees rose by 7 cents, or 0.2 percent, to $32.60.
(See tables B-3 and B-8.)
The average workweek for all employees on private nonfarm payrolls remained at 34.4 hours in
September.
In manufacturing, the average workweek was unchanged at 40.6 hours, and overtime held at
3.0 hours.
The average workweek for production and nonsupervisory employees on private nonfarm
payrolls remained at 33.8 hours.
(See tables B-2 and B-7.)
The change in total nonfarm payroll employment for July was revised down by 31,000, from +21,000 to
-10,000, and the change for August was revised down by 29,000, from +162,000 to +133,000.
With
these revisions, employment in July and August combined is 60,000 lower than previously reported.
(Monthly revisions result from additional reports received from businesses and government agencies
since the last published estimates and from the recalculation of seasonal factors.)

– October 27, 2026 – For the four weeks ending October 10, 2026, U.S.

These estimates are based on ADP's finely tuned, high-frequency data.
The data is seasonally adjusted and have a two-week lag to allow for more complete and accurate estimates of real-time employment trends.
The NER Pulse, including 12 weeks of historical data, publishes every Tuesday at 8:15 a.m.

THE EMPLOYMENT SITUATION - SEPTEMBER 2026
Both nonfarm payroll employment (+29,000) and the unemployment rate (4.2 percent) changed little in
September, the U.S.
Bureau of Labor Statistics reported today.
Employment in all major industries
changed little over the month.
This news release presents statistics from two monthly surveys.
The household survey measures labor
force status, including unemployment, by demographic characteristics.
The establishment survey
measures nonfarm employment, hours, and earnings by industry.
For more information about the
concepts and statistical methodology used in these two surveys, see the Technical Note.
Household Survey Data
Both the unemployment rate, at 4.2 percent, and the number of unemployed people, at 7.1 million,
changed little in September.
The unemployment rate has remained in a narrow range of 4.1 percent to
4.3 percent since March.
(See table A-1.)
Among the major worker groups, the unemployment rate for people who are Black (7.0 percent)
increased in September.
The jobless rates for adult men (3.9 percent), adult women (3.6 percent),
teenagers (14.5 percent), and people who are White (3.6 percent), Asian (2.9 percent), or Hispanic
(4.7 percent) showed little change over the month.
(See tables A-1, A-2, and A-3.)
The number of long-term unemployed (those jobless for 27 weeks or more) was essentially unchanged
at 1.9 million in September.
The long-term unemployed accounted for 27.1 percent of all unemployed
people.
(See table A-12.)
Both the labor force participation rate, at 61.8 percent, and the employment-population ratio, at
59.2 percent, changed little in September.
These measures showed little net change since January.
(See table A-1.)
The number of people employed part time for economic reasons changed little at 4.5 million in
September.
These individuals would have preferred full-time employment but were working part time
because their hours had been reduced or they were unable to find full-time jobs.

[...]
rage hourly earnings for all employees on private nonfarm payrolls edged up by 5
cents, or 0.1 percent, to $37.81.
Over the past 12 months, average hourly earnings have increased
by 3.0 percent.
In September, average hourly earnings of private-sector production and
nonsupervisory employees rose by 7 cents, or 0.2 percent, to $32.60.
(See tables B-3 and B-8.)
The average workweek for all employees on private nonfarm payrolls remained at 34.4 hours in
September.
In manufacturing, the average workweek was unchanged at 40.6 hours, and overtime held at
3.0 hours.
The average workweek for production and nonsupervisory employees on private nonfarm
payrolls remained at 33.8 hours.
(See tables B-2 and B-7.)
The change in total nonfarm payroll employment for July was revised down by 31,000, from +21,000 to
-10,000, and the change for August was revised down by 29,000, from +162,000 to +133,000.
With
these revisions, employment in July and August combined is 60,000 lower than previously reported.
(Monthly revisions result from additional reports received from businesses and government agencies
since the last published estimates and from the recalculation of seasonal factors.)
_____________

at 8:30 a.m.
(ET).

The U.S.
unemployment rate rose from 4.1% in August to 4.2% in September, a value similar to its 12-month average.

polymarket-5211634.text:
The U.S.
unemployment rate rose from 4.1% in August to 4.2% in September, a value similar to its 12-month average.
More precise data show the rate increased slightly from 4.141% to 4.175%.
The overall change is based on the precise unemployment rate for these periods; for example, the unemployment rates were 4.1754% in September and 4.1413% in August.

Flash Report: Unemployment Rises Slightly, Job Growth Slows in September
KEY TAKEAWAYS
- The U.S.
unemployment rate rose from 4.1% in August to 4.2% in September, a value similar to its 12-month average.
More precise data show the rate increased slightly from 4.141% to 4.175%.
- This very modest uptick was primarily driven by the combination of two offsetting forces: fewer unemployed people chose to stop looking for work and leave the labor force, and more unemployed people found jobs.
- Nonfarm payroll growth slowed in September to 29,000 jobs — less than half as many as forecasts expected.
Unemployment
September 2026

Precise Rate
Unemployment changed little in September, despite the rise in the headline rate to 4.2%.
(See the FRED chart above.) The more precise unemployment rate showed a much more modest increase.
Additionally, the labor force participation rate and employment-to-population ratio both improved again in September, albeit slightly.
The labor force participation rate rose 0.2 percentage points to 61.8% and the employment-to-population ratio rose 0.1 percentage points to 59.2%.
Total nonfarm payroll growth continued to be volatile from month to month.
The economy added a less-than-anticipated 29,000 jobs in September as payroll gains in August and 
[...]
he overall unemployment rate.
DATA HIGHLIGHTS
- While the headline unemployment rate ticked up to 4.2% in September, the unrounded rate shows a smaller, 0.03 percentage point increase from August.
- More unemployed people deciding to keep seeking work instead of leaving the workforce and more unemployed people finding jobs were the main factors behind the overall change in the unemployment rate.

The flow components into and out of unemployment add up to the change in unemployment with a negligible residual.
See Maximiliano Dvorkin and Serdar Ozkan’s St.

Compared with August, the 0.03 percentage point change in the unemployment rate was mostly due to the interplay between 1) lower-than-average transitions of unemployed people out of the labor force (e.g., discouraged workers), and 2) unemployed people finding jobs at a higher-than-average rate.
The first pushes the unemployment rate up, while the second pushes it down.
Other components of unemployment flows — people losing or leaving their jobs and people not in the labor force who began looking for work — were more in line with their recent averages.

October 28, 2026
Federal Reserve issues FOMC statement
For release at 2:00 p.m.
EDT
The Federal Open Market Committee approved the following statement for release by a 10 – 2 vote:
The Committee decided to maintain the target range for the federal funds rate at 3-3/4 to 4 percent, in support of the Federal Reserve's dual mandate.
The Committee is continuing its policy of maintaining ample reserves in the banking system.
Economic activity is expanding at a strong pace.
While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient.
Productivity growth is strong, and capital investment is robust.
Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little.
Inflation remains elevated.
The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee's 2 percent goal.
The Committee will deliver price stability.
Voting against the monetary policy action were Lisa D.
Cook and Beth M.
Hammack, who preferred to raise the target range for the federal funds rate by 1/4 percentage point at this meeting.

Personal income increased $54.5 billion (0.2 percent at a monthly rate) in September, according to estimates released today by the U.S.
Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA).
Disposable personal income (DPI)—personal income less personal current taxes—increased $52.7 billion (0.2 percent), and personal consumption expenditures (PCE) increased $113.1 billion (0.5 percent).
Personal outlays—the sum of PCE, personal interest payments, and personal current transfer payments—increased $113.0 billion in September.
Personal saving was $911.1 billion, and the personal saving rate—personal saving as a percentage of DPI—was 3.8 percent.
The increase in current-dollar personal income in September primarily reflected increases in compensation and government social benefits.
The $113.1 billion increase in current-dollar PCE in September reflected increases of $35.1 billion in spending on goods and $78.1 billion in spending on services.
Real PCE increased $2.6 billion (less than 0.1 percent at a monthly rate) in September.

Excluding food and energy, the PCE price index increased 0.3 percent.
