New Arizona poll shows Democrats leading in several key races
PHOENIX (AZFamily) — With three weeks until Election Day, a stunning new HighGround poll reveals Arizona Democrats leading Republicans in every major statewide race despite the GOP outnumbering Democrats by 300,000 registered voters statewide.
In the governor’s race, Gov.
Katie Hobbs leads Republican Andy Biggs by 17 points.
Secretary of State Adrian Fontes is up 12 points over Alexander Kolodin, and Attorney General Kris Mayes leads Warren Petersen by 15 points.
Democrats are also leading in the high single digits in the races for treasurer and superintendent.
Voters interviewed Tuesday pointed to President Donald Trump as the driving force.
“Even though I’m a registered Republican and always have been, I’m voting for the current governor, the incumbent,” Stan Taylor said over coffee with friend Kim Roberts, who also plans to vote for the incumbent.
“I do not like their leadership at all, and it’s frightening,” another voter said of Trump and the Republican Party.
HighGround President Chuck Coughlin, whose firm has repeatedly been named Arizona’s top pollster, said he stands by the findings.
He said 25-30% of Republican voters are not supporting their party’s candidates.
“In order to win a statewide election, you need 90 to 95% of your party to be supporting you, and that didn’t show up.
That shocked us,” Coughlin said.
“If you would have told me at the beginning of the year that you would have had the governor up 17 points with less than a month to go, I would have said that’s crazy.
Biggs’ campaign questioned the poll — not just the numbers, but the motivation.
A spokesperson noted Coughlin’s company works for a firm bankrolling pro-Hobbs attack ads.
“We did this with our money.
We didn’t ask anybody for any resources to do this.
We have a long history at HighGround of being interested in politics,” Coughlin responded.
For some Phoenix voters, the message to Biggs and the GOP ticket was blunt: “After this election, I believe the circus is leaving town, and the head clown will be gone,” Taylor said.

Where the race stands
Analysis
Gov.
Katie Hobbs (D), who narrowly won her first term in 2022, faces Rep.
Andy Biggs (R), a five-term congressman; Green and No Labels nominees are also on the ballot.
Biggs is running on affordability, the border, and water: he calls Hobbs an open borders advocate for defunding a state border strike force, and, in Colorado River talks, wants to tap Arizona's groundwater stores rather than rely mainly on conservation, and criticizes her record 541 vetoes.
His platform pledges to eliminate the state income tax, protect Empowerment Scholarship Accounts, and create a "Make Arizona Healthy Again" advisory council; in debate he said he would fund the tax cut partly by rooting out about $3 billion a year in Medicaid fraud.
He also backs a referendum to ban foreign contributions in Arizona elections.
Hobbs frames the race as steady leadership putting Arizona first against Washington-style division, and her ads have stressed her record on border security, law enforcement, and public safety.
Hobbs skipped the October 6 debate run by the Clean Elections Commission, saying face-to-face interactions with voters work better than a stage built for political theater; Biggs, who debated the No Labels nominee instead, called her absence "disqualifying." The air war has turned personal: Hobbs's campaign has run ads branding Biggs a "predator protector" over the Epstein files and over a bill, stalled while Biggs was Senate president, that targeted Warren Jeffs's hold on the Colorado City marshal's office, and Biggs has answered with an ad saying she vetoed bills aimed at "predators and pornographers." Hobbs is pressing Biggs on Medicaid: as a state senator in 2011 he tried to abolish Arizona's Medicaid program, and he voted for the 2025 federal budget law expected to drop a few hundred thousand Arizonans from it.
HighGround's Chuck Coughlin, releasing a mid-October survey with Hobbs up 17, said 25 to 30 percent of Republicans were not backing their party's candidates; the Biggs campaign questioned the poll because Coughlin's company works for a firm funding pro-Hobbs ads.
Arizona's narrow margins keep it a battleground, but Hobbs holds a clear edge in polls and markets.

No person shall be elected more than two times to each office of the executive branch of government: governor, lieutenant governor, secretary of state or attorney general.
This limitation on the number of times a person shall be elected to office shall apply to terms of office beginning on or after January 1, 1993.

MCL - Article V § 30
STATE CONSTITUTION (EXCERPT)
CONSTITUTION OF MICHIGAN OF 1963
§ 30 Limitations on terms of executive officers.
Sec.
30.
No person shall be elected more than two times to each office of the executive branch of government: governor, lieutenant governor, secretary of state or attorney general.
Any person appointed or elected to fill a vacancy in the office of governor, lieutenant governor, secretary of state or attorney general for a period greater than one half of a term of such office, shall be considered to have been elected to serve one time in that office for purposes of this section.
This limitation on the number of times a person shall be elected to office shall apply to terms of office beginning on or after January 1, 1993.
This section shall be self-executing.
Legislation may be enacted to facilitate operation of this section, but no law shall limit or restrict the application of this section.
If any part of this section is held to be invalid or unconstitutional, the remaining parts of this section shall not be affected but will remain in full force and effect.
History: Add.
Initiated Law, approved Nov.
3, 1992, Eff.
Dec.

Jocelyn Benson continues to lead over John James in new Michigan gubernatorial poll
Democrat Jocelyn Benson's lead over Republican John James in Michigan's gubernatorial contest appears to be narrowing, but holding up, among likely voters as Election Day approaches.
Mitchell Research & Communications conducted its latest statewide poll Oct.
26-27 for CBS Detroit and other Michigan television stations.
The researchers surveyed likely voters in the Nov.
3 general election, and issued a report on the gubernatorial race on Thursday.
The research company said Benson appears to be the choice of 49% of likely voters, with James at 44% in the late October survey.
In an early October poll, Benson was the choice of 46% of likely voters, with James at 39%.
The late October survey has a margin of error of 3.9%, the research company said, at the 95%+ confidence level.
The poll of 636 likely voters, using online panels along with survey links sent to randomly selected registered voters' cell phones, was weighted by demographics and 2022 and 2024 election results to project likely voter turnout in 2026.
"Benson maintains a clear advance in the race for Governor," the research company said.
"Strong support among women, younger voters, and African Americans continue to underpin her lead, while James remains competitive among men and older voters."
Mitchell Research & Communications also issued a follow-up poll on Michigan's closely watched U.S.
Senate race on Wednesday.
Casting votes and making decisions
By the time the second poll took place, more respondents had already voted by absentee ballot or early in person: 28% voter turnout in late October, compared with 11% in early October.
Absentee voting season had just started in Michigan when the first poll was conducted.
The second poll was conducted just after the early in-person voting season began in Michigan.
The campaign
The race is open because current Gov.
Gretchen Whitmer, a Democrat, is term-limited.
Benson and James then won their respective state party primaries in August.
She is currently Michigan's Secretary of State and announced her candidacy for this role in January 2025.
He is currently a U.S.
Congressman for Michigan's 10th district and announced his candidacy for this role in April 2025.
The third-party candidates appearing on the Nov.
3 ballot for this seat are Donna Brandenburg (U.S.
Taxpayers), Douglas Campbell (Green), and Anthony Hudson (who is listed on the ballot as a Libertarian, although the party has since disavowed him).
Benson and James met for a televised debate on Oct.
6 and again on Oct.
15.

East Lansing, Mich., October 26, 2026 – The Institute for Public Policy and Social Research (IPPSR) at Michigan State University released its new State of the State Survey today, showing Jocelyn Benson now leads John James 53.3% to 40.9% among likely voters in the race for governor.

MSU Poll Shows Benson with large lead while El-Sayed/ Roger race tight
.Anti-Muslim attitudes may be playing an important role in the Senate race.
East Lansing, Mich., October 26, 2026 – The Institute for Public Policy and Social Research (IPPSR) at Michigan State University released its new State of the State Survey today, showing Jocelyn Benson now leads John James 53.3% to 40.9% among likely voters in the race for governor.
The Senate contest is much tighter, with Abdul El-Sayed leading Mike Rogers 48% to 45.5%.
The August version of the survey had Benson up 9 percentage points on James and El-Sayed up 5.5 percentage points on Rogers.
The new survey shows more splits between Benson and El-Sayed.
Benson now outperforms El-Sayed, especially among independents, Wayne County residents, Catholics, Black voters, and ideological moderates.
Voters under 30 are the exception: El-Sayed runs ahead of Benson among them.
"The gap between the governor and Senate races has grown, with centrist voters more likely to support Benson than El-Sayed," said Dr.
Matt Grossmann, Director of IPPSR.
However, Islamophobia may also be a factor in the Senate race.
About 38% of voters say a Muslim candidate would make them less likely to offer support.
Those voters are much less likely to support El-Sayed, as are voters who rate Muslims negatively when asked their feelings toward the group.
Trump's unpopularity is a headwind for Republicans.
Only 35% of voters rate his performance as excellent or good, and 52% say a Trump endorsement makes them less likely to support a candidate.
YouGov conducted interviews for the Office for Survey Research (OSR) and IPPSR between October 2–19, 2026.
Each wave included 1,000 interviews; respondents were matched to a sampling frame of Michigan adults drawn from the 2023 American Community Survey, weighted by propensity score, and then post-stratified on 2024 presidential vote, gender, age, race, and education.
Full topline results of related questions are available here.
For more information about the State of the State Survey and for past results, please click here.

About Ethereum
Ethereum is a blockchain platform that enables developers to build and deploy smart contracts and decentralized applications, operating through thousands of independent nodes worldwide rather than through a central authority.
-
Smart Contract Pioneer: Ethereum introduced programmable smart contracts that automatically execute agreements when predetermined conditions are met, revolutionizing how digital transactions and applications function.
-
Proof of Stake Security: Following The Merge in September 2022, Ethereum transitioned from energy-intensive mining to an efficient Proof of Stake consensus mechanism, reducing energy consumption by over 99%.
-
Programmable Money: Ether (ETH) serves as both the native currency for transactions and the fuel that powers decentralized finance applications, NFT marketplaces, and thousands of decentralized applications across its ecosystem.
What Is the Difference Between Ethereum and Ether (ETH)?
-
Ethereum is the network.
It is the decentralized, global blockchain platform that runs smart contracts and supports applications.
Think of it as a global computer or an operating system.
-
Ether (ETH) is the cryptocurrency.
It is the native token or "fuel" of the Ethereum network.
ETH is used to pay transaction fees (known as "gas") and to secure the network through staking.
Ether is the asset that is bought, sold, and traded on exchanges.
How Does Ethereum Work?
Ethereum operates as a global, decentralized computer that executes programs called smart contracts.
The network consists of thousands of independent nodes operated by individuals and organizations worldwide, all maintaining a shared record of transactions and data.
When someone initiates a transaction or interacts with an application on Ethereum, validators process and confirm these actions, adding them to the blockchain permanently.
Unlike traditional centralized systems where a single entity controls operations, Ethereum distributes authority across its entire network.
This design ensures that no single party can manipulate transactions or shut down applications.
The network's native cryptocurrency, ether, serves multiple purposes: it pays for transaction fees, compensates validators for securing the network, and functions as collateral in various financial applications.
Smart Contracts & EVM
Smart contracts are self-executing programs stored on the Ethereum blockchain that automatically carry out agreements when specific conditions are met.
Written primarily in Solidity, a programming language designed for Ethereum, these contracts run on the Ethereum Virtual Machine, which acts as a global computing platform distributed across thousands of nodes.
The EVM ensures that smart contracts execute identically on every computer in the network, creating a trustworthy environment where outcomes are predictable and tamper-proof.
Developers can build anything from simple payment systems to complex financial instruments, gaming platforms, and decentralized organizations.
Once deployed, smart contracts operate autonomously without the need for intermediaries, and their code remains publicly verifiable on the blockchain.
This programmability distinguishes Ethereum from Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies focused solely on transferring value.
Applications built on Ethereum can hold and transfer assets, enforce rules, manage identities, and coordinate activities between multiple parties without traditional intermediaries like banks, brokers, or administrators.
Proof of Stake
Ethereum secures its network through Proof of Stake, a consensus mechanism that replaced the previous Proof of Work system in September 2022.
Under Proof of Stake, validators stake their ether (ETH) as collateral to participate in proposing and validating new blocks of transactions.
The network randomly selects validators to create blocks and confirm transactions based on their staked amount and other factors.
Validators earn rewards for honestly performing their duties but face penalties, known as slashing, if they act maliciously or fail to maintain their nodes properly.
This economic incentive structure ensures network security without requiring massive computational power.
A validator who attempts to approve fraudulent transactions or goes offline repeatedly risks losing a portion of their staked ether.
The transition to Proof of Stake brought multiple benefits.
Energy consumption dropped by approximately 99.95%, making Ethereum environmentally sustainable.
The mechanism also strengthened decentralization by lowering barriers to participation compared to the mining equipment required under Proof of Work.
Additionally, Proof of Stake established the foundation for future scalability improvements through technologies like danksharding.
How to Stake ETH
ETH holders can help secure the network and earn rewards by staking their ether.
Annual yields typically vary, often ranging between 3-5%.
Participants can choose different methods based on their technical skill and the amount of ETH they have.
Options range from running a dedicated 'solo' validator (which requires 32 ETH) , using a "staking as a service" provider , joining a pooled staking platform with a smaller amount, or using the staking services offered by centralized exchanges.
What Makes Ethereum Unique?
-
Programmable Platform: Unlike Bitcoin, which functions primarily as a digital currency, Ethereum operates as a global application platform where developers can create any type of decentralized service through smart contracts
-
Largest DeFi Ecosystem: The network hosts over $14 billion locked in DeFi applications, with hundreds of thousands of active users interacting with financial protocols, NFT marketplaces, gaming platforms, and social applications daily
-
True Decentralization: Thousands of independent validators operate globally with no central authority controlling development or operations, ensuring applications continue functioning regardless of jurisdictional restrictions
-
Developer Network Effect: The largest community of blockchain developers builds on Ethereum, creating a self-reinforcing cycle where more developers attract more users and applications
History of Ethereum
Vitalik Buterin proposed Ethereum in late 2013 as a blockchain platform that could support applications beyond simple currency transfers.
Buterin envisioned a network where developers could build decentralized versions of traditional services using smart contracts.
Following a crowdfunding campaign in mid-2014 that raised over $18 million, Ethereum launched its mainnet in July 2015.
The network gained attention in 2017 when Initial Coin Offerings built on Ethereum raised billions of dollars for blockchain projects.

Crypto giant Binance hit by $6.3bn hack suspected to be largest in history
Cryptocurrency giant Binance said on Thursday that $6.3bn (£4.7bn) of digital assets have been impacted by what is thought to be the biggest crypto hack on record.
The world's biggest crypto exchange said about half of those assets had been frozen but that many remained in the hands of the hackers, adding that it will "cover all losses".
The firm said while initial checks suggested an engineer's laptop had been compromised, allowing an attacker to make unauthorised withdrawals, "our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach".
Two analytics firms have attributed the incident, which eclipses a record-setting $1.5bn hack on the Bybit exchange in 2025, to a North Korean hacking unit called TraderTraitor.
Cyber-security firm Check Point said the unit is also known in the industry as Lazarus Group, which has been blamed for the 2025 hack.
Check Point's chief information security officer Jayant Dave said the losses estimated by Binance made it "the largest crypto theft on record".
AI-powered investigations company TRM Labs said in a report that several elements of the Binance attack resemble earlier North Korean-linked incidents, including the Bybit hack.

"That gave an attacker access to a service container, where they submitted unauthorized withdrawal transactions," he said in a statement.
"To be clear: the attacker did not simply use one engineer's permissions, and this was not a single 'one-click' action.
It involved a more complex attack process.
Our investigation has not attributed responsibility to any individual.
So far, we have found no evidence of any wallet private key leak."
He said a detailed "post-mortem" would be shared once the investigation was complete.
In an update, the company said in a statement on X that another investigation found there had been other breach points: "We are still gathering the facts, and will share more directly as we have them."
Check Point's Dave said this attack also resembled a hack on crypto exchange platform Bitget in September in which $388m (£289m) was lost: "This implies that attackers no longer need the vault keys.
They target the systems and people with authority to use them."
In a series of posts, Yi He, Binance's co-chief executive, thanked various cryptocurrency issuers for freezing the assets.
"Safety first: withdrawals are currently disabled until the environment is confirmed to be secure," she said.
Two other major crypto platforms, Tether and Circle, said they had frozen a total of about $2.4bn of assets in response to the potential Binance hack.
World Liberty Financial, a crypto company linked to US President Donald Trump and his family, said it has worked with its partners to freeze stolen funds.
Crypto exchange Coinbase said it was unaffected by the incident and was monitoring the situation.
Several crypto industry observers had flagged concerns about a potential hack on Binance hours before the exchange confirmed the security issue.
Bitcoin dropped by more than 4% following the alerts.
The price of other major cryptocurrencies including Ethereum and Solana also fell sharply.

The Federal Open Market Committee approved the following statement for release by a 10 – 2 vote:
The Committee decided to maintain the target range for the federal funds rate at 3-3/4 to 4 percent, in support of the Federal Reserve's dual mandate.
The Committee is continuing its policy of maintaining ample reserves in the banking system.
Economic activity is expanding at a strong pace.
While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient.
Productivity growth is strong, and capital investment is robust.
Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little.
Inflation remains elevated.
The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee's 2 percent goal.
The Committee will deliver price stability.
Voting against the monetary policy action were Lisa D.
Cook and Beth M.
Hammack, who preferred to raise the target range for the federal funds rate by 1/4 percentage point at this meeting.

Independent Ty Pinkins says he is staying in Mississippi US Senate race
Some Democratic supporters have urged Pinkins to step aside, but ballots are already printed
JACKSON, Miss.
(WLBT) - Independent candidate Ty Pinkins said he will stay in the race for Mississippi’s U.S.
Senate seat after some Democratic supporters urged him to step aside.
They said his presence on the ballot could hurt Democratic nominee Scott Colom’s chances against Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith.
“I’m not going to concede my rights to run for office when I fully participated in protecting this democratic process when I served for 21 years,” Pinkins said.
“I will not do it, and I will not apologize for that.”
Calls to step aside
Community advocate Pauline Rogers is among those urging Pinkins to change course.
She wrote an open letter to Pinkins this past week.
“We have to bring all the people to the table who have a perspective what it’s like living among people who are suffering from all these different issues,” Rogers said.
“And Scott Colom is better positioned to bring that political reconstruction historically to the state of Mississippi if Ty Pinkins would move and do the right thing.”
Pinkins pushed back on that suggestion.
“I think that’s the most illogical thing that someone can tell someone — that every vote that I have is guaranteed to go to the Democrat if I get out of the race, refusing to see what just happened in 2020, 2018, all the way back to 1982,” Pinkins said.
“15 straight losses.”
Political scientist weighs in
Glenn Antizzo, a political science professor at Mississippi Christian University, said a third candidate offers an outlet for Mississippians tired of partisan gridlock.
“I’m not too worried about him being a spoiler in the race,” Antizzo said.
“And to be honest with you, it’s sort of refreshing to have a third person in the race.
I think a lot of people are getting very tired of the extremes in both parties.”
Antizzo said he still believes Republican base loyalty will remain strong on Election Day.
“I’m not saying that Senator Hyde-Smith is going to win a reelection in a landslide,” Antizzo said.
“I think that this may end up being like it was in the last governor’s race, a fairly narrow margin of victory.”
Ballots already printed
For Pinkins, staying on the ballot is about honoring petition signers across the state who wanted another option.
Under Mississippi law, official ballots are already printed.
Pinkins’ name will appear on the ballot with Hyde-Smith and Colom on Nov.
3, regardless of any calls to step down.

Mississippi Senate race gains national spotlight with high-profile campaign stops
The U.S.
Senate race in Mississippi between Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith and Democratic challenger Scott Colom is drawing national attention, with prominent campaign stops and debates over voter turnout and economic concerns.
President Donald Trump visited Corinth on Monday to campaign for Hyde-Smith, while former President Bill Clinton is scheduled to visit Tupelo later this week to support Colom.
Jackson State University political science professor Dr.
D’Andra Orey said economic conditions, including high gas and food prices, could influence voter behavior in the deep-red state.
“I think the race is close.
The race is close because of the economic conditions.
I mean, folks may not vote Democrat.
We're in a red state, deep red state, and folks may not vote Democrat,” Orey said.
Orey added that voters who are reluctant to support a Democrat in Mississippi might choose to stay home, but economic struggles could help Democrats mobilize their base.
One recent poll showed Hyde-Smith leading Colom by just three points, while other surveys indicate Hyde-Smith is ahead by a larger margin.
“All the indicators are that the Colom race are closer than some of the polls are suggesting, and that we are within striking distance — three points or better,” said Cheikh Taylor, a Democratic strategist.
Opinions on the closeness of the race vary among party leaders.
“I think it depends on which Republicans you ask.
Some think that it's close, and some think no, it's not at all.
It's just the same as what's been said before,” said Pete Perry, a Republican strategist.
Orey emphasized that voter turnout could ultimately determine the outcome of the race.
“People typically may not turn out to vote when they see that the race is close.
They may actually end up turning out because they don't want to see, again, they lose.
I guess my question was, do you think the race is close, or is it the perception that the race is close?” Orey said.
Whichever campaign can mobilize its supporters and get them to the polls could walk away victorious once all the votes are counted.

Get to know the candidates running for U.S.
Senate in Mississippi
BILOXI, Miss.
(WLOX) — Three candidates are vying for one of Mississippi’s seats in the U.S.
Senate in the general election.
Voters will choose among Republican incumbent U.S.
Sen.
Cindy Hyde-Smith, Democrat Scott Colom, and Independent Ty Pinkins.
The election is Tuesday, Nov.
3, and the polls will be open from 7 a.m.
to 7 p.m.
Sen.
Cindy Hyde-Smith
Hyde-Smith said gas and food prices are the two issues she hears about most from Mississippians.
The senator referenced a previous WLOX interview in which she drew attention for saying there are “other proteins to choose from.”
“Gasoline, unless you want to ride the bicycle, that’s your only option,” she said, adding that her earlier comment referred to consumers having cheaper protein options when shopping for meat.
“Thank goodness, when mothers want to feed their families, when you go out shopping there are proteins, you want to feed meat, there are some cheaper prices.
And that’s what that statement was about because there’s nothing to replace that gasoline unless you want to ride a bicycle,” Hyde-Smith said.
Hyde-Smith also said she has brought “two trillion dollars and over 365 projects to Mississippi.”
Scott Colom
Colom said tariffs, affordability and health care are big focuses of his campaign.
“The tariffs are a sales tax.
They’re a tax on everything.
And we’ve been paying more because of those tariffs,” he said.
Colom said one of his priorities would be reversing Medicaid cuts and restoring federal support for the Affordable Care Act.
“Day one, I’m going to fight to restore the Medicaid cuts, restore subsidy for people getting health insurance,” he said.
“In the long term, we’ve got to find some public option.
There needs to be competition with the insurance companies so people can either buy into some public, non-profit option, maybe buy into Medicare or Medicaid.”
Colom also said he supports eliminating federal income tax for anyone making under $75,000 a year, a policy he said would help government employees and others struggling financially.
Ty Pinkins
Pinkins, who is running as an independent, said neither political party aligns with him “morally.”
“I think there’s an integrity issue associated with that, and the only way that we can move forward in this country, I believe, is if we send Independents to Washington, particularly in the United States Senate,” Pinkins said.
Pinkins is a veteran and said the skills he learned in the military make him a quality candidate.
“I spent 21 years in the military,” Pinkins said.
“Fought for the specific rights that I’m using right now.
I finished the military and got two law degrees from Georgetown University and came back to Mississippi.”
Pinkins said some of the issues he plans to address are health care, housing, education, and affordability.
“The cost of housing didn’t just rise this year.
The cost of health care didn’t explode this month.
The cost of our kids’ education didn’t just go up this semester.
This has been going on for decades,” he said.
“The only thing that’s remained constant over those five decades, since 1973, is the same two parties have switched turns holding power in Washington.”

St.
Pete Polls surveyed 916 likely voters Oct.
25-27 for Florida Politics
At the registration split, it is 47% to 46%.

U.S.
Sen.
Ashley Moody leads Democrat Angie Nixon 49% to 45% in a new St.
Pete Polls survey for Florida Politics, her widest lead in three surveys by the pollster.
The sample is weighted 12 points Republican.
Ballots cast through Tuesday morning run Republican by less than one.
Another 3% picked someone else and 4% are undecided.
The margin of error is plus or minus 3.2 percentage points.
Republicans outnumber Democrats on the rolls by roughly 1.5 million, 5.69 million to 4.15 million at the Oct.
5 book closing, with 3.35 million more registered to no party.
The rolls are R+8.
The sample is R+12.
St.
Pete Polls’ mid-September survey had the race tied at 45%.
Its Oct.
5-7 survey had Moody ahead 47% to 45%.
Undecided voters have gone from 7% to 6% to 4%.
Nixon leads 56% to 41% among respondents who have already voted.
Moody leads 57% to 34% among those who have not.
Three in five Republican respondents said they had not voted yet.
Fewer than half of Democrats said the same.
Through Tuesday morning, Republicans had cast 40% of the 3.15 million ballots returned statewide and Democrats 39%, per the Division of Elections.
Voters outside the two parties cast the other 21%.
Democrats also hold more of the mail ballots still in circulation, 403,076 to 324,499.
In 2022, Republicans had out-voted Democrats by about 177,000 ballots at the same point in the calendar.
Reweighted to R+10, the same responses give Moody 48% to 45%.
At the registration split, it is 47% to 46%.
Nixon leads independents 53% to 36%, up from 49% to 36% in the October survey and 50% to 37% in September.
Moody holds 84% of Republicans, up from 82%.
Nixon holds 83% of Democrats, unchanged.
Men back Moody 50% to 43% after favoring Nixon 48% to 45% in October.
Women back Moody 49% to 45%.
Voters 70 and older back Moody 66% to 29%.
Nixon leads voters under 30 by 64% to 28%, those 30 to 49 by 52% to 39%, and those 50 to 69 by 48% to 46%.
White voters favor Moody 59% to 35%.
Black voters favor Nixon 77% to 17%, and Hispanic voters favor her 51% to 41%.
Moody leads the Tampa market 51% to 42%, Jacksonville 52% to 39%, Orlando 50% to 44%, West Palm Beach 48% to 46%, and Fort Myers 62% to 33%.
Nixon leads Miami 49% to 46%.
The University of North Florida’s survey released last week had the same numbers, Moody 49% to 45%.
St.
Pete Polls surveyed 916 likely voters Oct.
25-27 for Florida Politics, using automated phone calls for 71% of responses and peer-to-peer text messages for 29%.
Respondents were drawn at random from the state’s registered voter file as of Oct.
14.
Results were weighted by political party, race, age, gender, and media market to match Florida’s active voter population.
The weighted sample is 43% Republican, 31% Democratic, and 27% other.
Voters who said they do not plan to vote in the General Election were excluded.
The margin of error is plus or minus 3.2 percentage points at a 95% confidence level.

U.S.
Sen.
Ashley Moody holds a lead on Democrat Angie Nixon in the highly respected New York Times/Siena University poll.
Perhaps more important, it shows the Republican appointed incumbent at the critical 50% support level.
That survey shows the Plant City Republican as the preference of 50% of likely voters, while 44% favor the Democratic challenger.
The same poll also shows Republican Byron Donalds winning 48% of the vote to Democrat David Jolly’s 44%.
According to the Times index of publicly available polling, the Moody lead is consistent with other pollsters’ findings.
The numbers were published the same day as a Florida Politics-commissioned poll by St.
Pete Polls showing a more modest lead of 49% to 45% for Moody.
Additionally, ActVote published a survey with a more robust Moody lead of 53% to 47%.
The St.
Pete Polls survey found Donalds leading Jolly by a narrow 48% to 46%.
New York Times analyst Nate Cohn said the polling was the least surprising result from Siena of the day.
The pollster also found a tied Senate race in South Carolina between Republican Darline Graham and Democrat Annie Andrews and a 14-percentage-point lead for Democrat Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota.
“It’s worth observing that the poll suggests there will be a relatively robust turnout of Florida Republicans — reflecting the turnout history of Republicans in the state, even though Democrats have gotten off to a strong start in early voting,” Cohn wrote.
The poll of 813 Florida voters was conducted from Oct.
19-26, and pollsters report a 3.9-percentage-point margin of error.
Of note, the same pollsters in early October 2024 found Republican U.S.
Sen.
Rick Scott leading Democrat Debbie Mucarsel-Powell 49% to 40%, a wider margin than Moody currently enjoys but still putting the incumbent under 50%.
Scott ultimately won the race by nearly 13 percentage points.
The most surprising finding from the new poll may not be Moody’s lead but that it suggests the electorate in Florida will lean 13 percentage points Republican in terms of turnout.
That suggests far more Republicans will vote than have already done so by mail or through in-person voting.
Democratic strategist Steve Schale on Tuesday noted that GOP turnout in the state is below 2022 levels while Democratic and nonpartisan turnout is up, though he stressed observers should not read too much into early voting numbers.
